segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: I agreed to spend seven days using a basic phone that could only call and send texts. I expected boredom. What surprised me first was how often I reached for a smartphone without any clear reason: in lifts, in queues and even while waiting for a friend who was only two minutes late.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: The first two days felt inefficient. I had to write directions on paper and check train times before leaving home. But by the middle of the week I noticed a different problem: I had been using convenience to avoid small moments of uncertainty. If I did not know something immediately, I normally searched for it.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: The experiment was not magical. I missed group messages, and arranging a last-minute meeting was genuinely harder. I also borrowed my laptop for schoolwork, so I was not completely offline.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: When the week ended, I happily returned to my smartphone. The change is that I turned off most non-essential notifications and stopped carrying the phone from room to room at home. I did not learn that technology is bad. I learned that convenience can become automatic before you notice what habit it has created.

options: The basic phone had no battery.
How often the speaker reached for a smartphone without a clear purpose.
Friends refused to send texts.
Train journeys became shorter.
questions.explanationJa: 明確な目的がなくても頻繁にsmartphoneへ手を伸ばしていたことです。

questions.prompt: Give two examples of tasks that became less convenient.
markscheme: Writing down directions / navigating without a smartphone.
Checking train times in advance and/or arranging last-minute meetings.
questions.explanationJa: directions、train times、last-minute meetingなどが不便になりました。

questions.prompt: The speaker says convenience had been used to avoid small moments of ________.
questions.explanationJa: すぐ検索することでuncertaintyを避けていたと気づきます。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO limits of the experiment.
options: The speaker missed group messages.
The speaker stopped all schoolwork.
Last-minute plans were harder.
The speaker had no access to any computer.
The experiment lasted a year.
questions.explanationJa: group messagesとlast-minute plansが実際に困難でした。

questions.prompt: What change did the speaker make afterward?
options: Giving up smartphones permanently
Turning off most non-essential notifications
Deleting all school apps
Buying two phones
questions.explanationJa: non-essential notificationsを多くoffにしました。

questions.prompt: What lesson does the speaker emphasize?
options: Technology is always harmful.
Convenience can quietly create automatic habits.
Basic phones are better for schoolwork.
Uncertainty should always be avoided.
questions.explanationJa: technology否定ではなく、convenienceが無意識のhabitを作る点が結論です。

title: My first month as a mentor

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Sixth-form student Hana has spent a month mentoring younger students who have just joined the school. Hana, what did you expect the role to involve?

segments.speaker: Hana
segments.text: I thought people would ask obvious questions about timetables and classrooms. They did, but the hardest questions were smaller: where to sit at lunch, how to join a club if you do not know anyone, or what to do when everyone else seems more confident.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: How did you respond?

segments.speaker: Hana
segments.text: At first I gave too much advice. I wanted to solve every problem. One student finally said, 'I just wanted to know if this feeling is normal.' That changed the way I listened. Sometimes reassurance is more useful than a list of instructions.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Did mentoring change how you see your own first year?

segments.speaker: Hana
segments.text: Definitely. I had forgotten how many routines are invisible once you know them. Even finding the right queue in the cafeteria can feel stressful when everything is new. Now I notice how much belonging depends on small pieces of information that older students take for granted.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Will you continue?

segments.speaker: Hana
segments.text: Yes, but I want the programme to involve more mentors. One person cannot know every club, subject or social situation. A network is more useful than pretending one mentor has every answer.

questions.prompt: What kinds of questions surprised Hana?
options: Only questions about exams
Small social and practical questions about belonging
Questions about university applications
Questions about teachers' salaries
questions.explanationJa: lunchやclubなど、belongingに関わる小さな質問が意外に重要でした。

questions.prompt: Give two examples of questions younger students asked.
markscheme: Where to sit at lunch and/or how to join a club without knowing anyone.
What to do when everyone else seems more confident.

questions.prompt: What changed Hana's approach to mentoring?
options: A teacher told her to speak less.
A student said they mainly wanted reassurance that their feeling was normal.
The programme was cancelled.
She changed schools.
questions.explanationJa: studentの『この気持ちは普通か知りたい』という言葉が転機です。

options: Familiar routines can be invisible to experienced students.
Every problem needs a long list of advice.
Small pieces of information can support belonging.
One mentor can know every possible answer.
New students never worry about lunch.
questions.explanationJa: routineの見えにくさとsmall informationの重要性です。

questions.prompt: Hana says a ________ is more useful than pretending one mentor has every answer.
questions.explanationJa: 複数mentorのnetworkが必要だと述べています。

questions.prompt: What is Hana's attitude toward the programme?
options: She wants to stop immediately.
She supports it but wants broader participation from mentors.

questions.explanationJa: programmeを支持しつつmentor数を増やしたい立場です。

title: The journey that refused to go to plan

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Travel journalist Marcus Lee is telling us about a trip that went wrong before it properly began. Marcus, what happened?

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: A storm cancelled my flight, and the replacement left the next afternoon. I had arranged an interview for that morning, so my first reaction was panic. I treated the delay as if the entire assignment had failed.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Did you manage to save the interview?

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: Yes. I called the person instead of sending a long apology by email. We moved the interview to the final day. That direct conversation solved the practical problem in five minutes, although I had spent nearly an hour imagining every possible disaster.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: And the extra day at the airport?

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: I used part of it to rewrite my questions. I realized some were designed to show how much research I had done rather than to get interesting answers. The delay forced me to simplify them.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: So was the cancellation actually a good thing?

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: I would not romanticize it. Delays cost people money and can cause serious problems. I was lucky that my schedule could move. But the experience reminded me to separate inconvenience from catastrophe, and to solve the problem in front of me before inventing five more.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: A useful distinction: learning from disruption without pretending disruption is harmless.

questions.prompt: Why did Marcus panic after the cancellation?
options: He lost his luggage permanently.
He had an interview scheduled for the next morning.
He had never flown before.
The airport closed for a month.
questions.explanationJa: 翌朝のinterviewに間に合わないためpanicしました。

questions.prompt: Give two actions Marcus took to recover from the disruption.
markscheme: He called the interviewee and rearranged the interview.
He used the extra time to rewrite / simplify his interview questions.
questions.explanationJa: interviewの再調整とquestionsの書き直しです。

questions.prompt: What did Marcus realize about some of his original questions?
options: They were too short to understand.
They were partly designed to display his research rather than invite good answers.
They were written in the wrong language.
They had already been published.
questions.explanationJa: 良いanswerを得るより、自分のresearch量を見せる質問になっていたと気づきます。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO qualifications Marcus makes about travel disruption.
options: Delays can cost people money.
Every delay becomes a valuable adventure.
Some people face serious consequences from delays.
Schedules are always flexible.
Airlines should stop giving replacement flights.
questions.explanationJa: delayにはcostやserious problemがあり、単純に良い経験とは言いません。

questions.prompt: What two mental habits does Marcus say he wants to change?
markscheme: Solve the immediate problem before imagining additional disasters / problems.
questions.explanationJa: inconvenienceとcatastropheを区別し、目の前のproblemから解くことです。

questions.prompt: What is the host's final purpose?
options: To challenge Marcus's facts
To summarize a balanced lesson from the story
To advertise the airport
To argue that cancelled flights are harmless
questions.explanationJa: disruptionから学びつつ害を美化しない、というbalanced lessonをまとめています。
